### cavity2d

This app is the simplified version of [[`laminar/cavity2d`](/examples/laminar/cavity2d.qmd)]{.content-visible when-format="html"}[`laminar/cavity2d` (@sec-example-laminar-cavity2d)]{.content-visible when-format="pdf"}. It contains the bare minimum code to execute the cavity benchmark case with $\OpenLB$. This example is suited to grasp the basic structure of $\OpenLB$ example cases.
This case is also used for the tutorial exercises at the $\OpenLB$ spring school.


#### Governing equations

The domain $\Omega \times \I \subseteq [0,1]^2 \times \R_{\geq 0}$ is considered with the following governing equations with the velocity field $\vel \in \R^2$ and the pressure $p \in \R$ for the incompressible flow of a Newtonian fluid with kinematic viscosity $\nu \in \R_{> 0}$ and constant density $\rho \in \R_{> 0}$,
\begin{align}
    \nabla \cdot \vel &= 0 \quad \text{in} \quad \Omega \times \I, \\
    \partial_t \vel + (\vel \cdot \nabla) \vel &= -\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p + \nu \Delta \vel \quad \text{in} \quad \Omega \times \I.
\end{align}

#### Boundary conditions

The boundary $\partial \Omega = \Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}}$ consists of two parts (@fig-cavity2d-domain): the moving lid $\Gamma_D$ at the top, where the lid velocity is prescribed as a Dirichlet condition, and the three walls at rest $\Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}}$, where the fluid sticks to the wall,
\begin{align}
    \vel &= (u_\text{lid}, 0)^\top \quad \text{on} \quad \Gamma_D \times \I, \\
    \vel &= \mathbf{0} \quad \text{on} \quad \Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}} \times \I.
\end{align}
The fluid is initially at rest, $\vel = \mathbf{0}$ in $\Omega$ at $t = 0$.
In `prepareGeometry()`, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}}$ gets the material number 2 and $\Gamma_D$ the material number 3; the two top corners belong to the lid.

#### Domain

The fluid fills a square cavity of side length $L = 1\,\mathrm{m}$ (@fig-cavity2d-domain).
The lid at the top moves with $u_\text{lid} = 1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $x$-direction, while the remaining three walls are at rest.
With $\nu = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$ this gives a Reynolds number of $Re = u_\text{lid} L / \nu = 1000$.

![Domain and boundary conditions of `cavity2d`, with the material numbers (MN) assigned in `prepareGeometry()`.](/examples/forBeginners/cavity2d/docs/fig/cavity2dDomain.svg){width="60%" #fig-cavity2d-domain .lightbox}

#### Discretization \& Descriptor
In this example, the domain is discretized with a uniform grid of $N^2$ cells with the lattice spacing $\Delta x = L / N$, where the default is $N = 128$.

The LBM collision operator is the BGK operator with a single relaxation time ([Collision Operators](/content/02_core.qmd#collision-operators)), used as `ConstRhoBGKdynamics`, together with the D2Q9 velocity set ([Lattice Structures](/content/01_introduction.qmd#sec-lattice-structures)).
All four walls, including the moving lid, are velocity boundaries of the type `InterpolatedVelocity` ([Define Boundary Method](/content/06_initial_boundary.qmd#sec-defineBoundaryMethod)).

The parameters for the simulation are given in @tbl-cavity2d-params.

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DOMAIN_EXTENT` | $L \times L$ | $1\,\mathrm{m} \times 1\,\mathrm{m}$ | side lengths of the cavity |
| `PHYS_DELTA_X` | $\Delta x$ | $7.8125 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$ | lattice spacing, $L / 128$ |
| `PHYS_DELTA_T` | $\Delta t$ | $7.8125 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s}$ | time step size |
| `PHYS_CHAR_VELOCITY` | $u_\text{lid}$ | $1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ | velocity of the lid |
| `PHYS_CHAR_VISCOSITY` | $\nu$ | $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$ | kinematic viscosity |
| `PHYS_CHAR_DENSITY` | $\rho$ | $1\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ | density |
| `MAX_PHYS_T` | $T$ | $30\,\mathrm{s}$ | simulated time, $38\,400$ time steps |
| `PHYS_ITER_T` | | $1.5\,\mathrm{s}$ | interval of the console statistics and timer reports |

: Parameters of `cavity2d`, as set in `main()`. {#tbl-cavity2d-params}

::: {#lst-cavity2d-descriptor}

using MyCase = Case<
  NavierStokes, Lattice<double, descriptors::D2Q9<>>
>;

#### Validation

The example writes the velocity and the pressure in physical units every $T/100 = 0.3\,\mathrm{s}$.
@fig-example-cavity shows the velocity magnitude: the lid drives a primary vortex that fills most of the cavity, with a thin boundary layer below the lid and the strongest return flow along the right wall.
This simplified example does not compare against reference data.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![Magnitude of the physical velocity of `cavity2d` from $t = 0.3\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t = 29.7\,\mathrm{s}$, visualized in ParaView. The vortex starts in the upper right corner below the lid and moves towards the center of the cavity.](/examples/forBeginners/cavity2d/docs/fig/cavity2d_velocity.gif){width="100%" #fig-example-cavity .lightbox}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![Magnitude of the physical velocity of `cavity2d`, visualized in ParaView.](/examples/forBeginners/cavity2d/docs/fig/cavity_vel_magnitude.png){width="100%" #fig-example-cavity .lightbox}
:::

#### Files

```
cavity2d/
├── cavity2d.cpp   main(): parameters, then mesh, geometry, lattice, initial values and time loop
└── Makefile
```

The results are written to `tmp/vtkData/` in the directory the example is run from; open `cavity2d.pvd` in ParaView to load all time steps.
